name: רציפה בלי נגזרת חלקית לפי x בראשית – x·sin(20/(x+y)) (באנגלית)
questiontext:
In this exercise and the few that follow it, we will discuss continuity, partial derivatives and differentiability of functions that are not elementary at the origin. Take for example the function

Let

\( f(x,y)=\left\{\begin{array}{cc}{{CT:0}} & (x,y)\neq (0,0) \\0 & (x,y)=(0,0)\end{array}\right. \)

Here is the graph of this function. It was created by typing "x*sin(20/(x+y))" at a google bar. Before going on, please take a few minutes and try it out yourself!

First, calculate the partial derivatives of \(f(x,y)\) when \((x,y)\neq (0,0)\).

\(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x,y)=\) [[input:ans1]]
[[validation:ans1]]
\(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x,y)=\) [[input:ans2]]
[[validation:ans2]]

Remark: The answer will be Printed as the program interprets it, please verify it's as expected.

Is \(f(x,y)\) continuous on its domain?

[[input:ans3]]
[[validation:ans3]]

Now calculate the partial derivatives at zero. If they do not exist, please enter "false"

\(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(0,0)=\) [[input:ans5]]
[[validation:ans5]]
\(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(0,0)=\) [[input:ans6]]
[[validation:ans6]]

Does a continuous function always have partial derivatives?

[[input:ans4]]
[[validation:ans4]]
generalfeedback:
Outline: Differentiate away from the origin; describe the domain and prove continuity on it (at the origin with the bound \(|\sin t|\le1\)); compute the partial derivatives at the origin from the definition along the axes.
Step 1 — Partial derivatives away from the origin
Where \(x+y eq0\), by the product and chain rules, with \(\left( rac{20}{x+y} ight)'_x=\left( rac{20}{x+y} ight)'_y=- rac{20}{(x+y)^2}\):

\[ rac{\partial f}{\partial x}=\sin rac{20}{x+y}+x\cos rac{20}{x+y}\cdot\left(- rac{20}{(x+y)^2} ight)=\sin rac{20}{x+y}- rac{20x}{(x+y)^2}\cos rac{20}{x+y} \]

\[ rac{\partial f}{\partial y}=x\cos rac{20}{x+y}\cdot\left(- rac{20}{(x+y)^2} ight)=- rac{20x}{(x+y)^2}\cos rac{20}{x+y} \]

Step 2 — Continuity on the domain
Domain: the formula is defined where \(x+y eq0\), and \(f\) is also defined at the origin (\(f(0,0)=0\)). So the domain is \(\{(x,y):x+y eq0\}\cup\{(0,0)\}\); the line \(x+y=0\) (apart from the origin) is not part of it. At every point of the domain other than the origin \(f\) is a composition of elementary functions, hence continuous. At the origin we take the limit as \((x,y) o(0,0)\) within the domain. The sine is bounded by 1, so

\[ 0\le|f(x,y)|=|x|\left|\sin rac{20}{x+y} ight|\le|x|\xrightarrow[(x,y) o(0,0)]{}0 \]

By the squeeze theorem \(\lim_{(x,y) o(0,0)}f(x,y)=0=f(0,0)\): \(f\) is continuous at the origin too, so \(f\) is continuous on its domain.
Step 3 — Partial derivatives at the origin, from the definition
On the \(x\)-axis \(f(h,0)=h\sin rac{20}{h}\), so

\[ rac{\partial f}{\partial x}(0,0)=\lim_{h o0} rac{h\sin rac{20}{h}-0}{h}=\lim_{h o0}\sin rac{20}{h} \]

This limit does not exist: for \(h_n= rac{20}{2\pi n} o0\) the sine equals 0, and for \(h_n= rac{20}{\pi/2+2\pi n} o0\) it equals 1. So \( rac{\partial f}{\partial x}(0,0)\) does not exist (enter false). On the \(y\)-axis \(f(0,h)=0\), so

\[ rac{\partial f}{\partial y}(0,0)=\lim_{h o0} rac{0-0}{h}=0 \]

Step 4 — Does a continuous function always have partial derivatives?
No. \(f\) itself is a counterexample: it is continuous at the origin, but \( rac{\partial f}{\partial x}(0,0)\) does not exist.

\[ rac{\partial f}{\partial x}(0,0)\ ext{does not exist},\qquad rac{\partial f}{\partial y}(0,0)=0 \]

on_true.feedback: Continuity on the domain: Correct answer, \(f(x,y)\) is indeed continuous. At every point of the domain other than the origin (that is, where \(x+y\neq0\)), \(f(x,y)\) is an elementary function, therefore continuous. And for \((x,y)=(0,0) \) \( \lim_{(x,y)\to(0,0)}x \cdot sin(\frac{20}{x+y})=0=f(0,0) \), therefore also continuous at \((0,0)\).

on_false.feedback: Continuity on the domain: Incorrect answer, \(f(x,y)\) is continuous. It is definitely continuous at any point \((x,y) \ne (0,0)\) of its domain (where \(x+y\neq0\)). And it turns out that it is continuous at the origin too. Try calculating the limit and find out for yourself. You can use the fact that \(\left| sin(20/(x+y)) \right| < 1\).

on_true.feedback: Does a continuous function always have partial derivatives: Your answer is correct. Our function here \(f(x,y)=\){{CT:1}} is an example. For \((x,y)=(0,0) f\) is continuous, but \( \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(0,0)=\lim_{h\to 0} \frac{f(h,0)-f(0,0)}{h}=\lim_{h\to 0} sin(\frac{20}{h}) \), therefore \( \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(0,0)\) doesn't exist.

on_false.feedback: Does a continuous function always have partial derivatives: Your answer is incorrect. In fact our function here is a counterexample. If you answer all the other questions correctly you will see that this is a continuous function that does not admit a well defined partial derivative in the \(x\) direction.

on_true.feedback: \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(0,0) \): Indeed this partial derivative is not defined. When we try to evaluate it we substitute \(y=0\) and differentiating with respect to \(x\). Thus obtaining the derivative \(= \frac{d}{dx} x sin(\frac{20}{x})\). And (hopefully) we remember from calculus one that this derivative does not exist.

on_false.feedback: \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(0,0) \): Please try again. Remember to evaluate \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(0,0) \) we have to substitute \(y=0\) and differentiate the resulting function of \(x\) with respect to \(x\).

on_true.feedback: \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(0,0) \): Your answer is correct. To evaluate \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(0,0) \) we have to substitute \(x=0\) and then differentiate the resulting function. What we get, is the easiest function to differentiate. \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(0,0) = \frac{d}{dy} 0_{y=0} = 0 \). Note that we found a function that has one partial derivative but not the other. Do go back to the graph of the function now and see if you understand how this happens!

on_false.feedback: \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(0,0) \): Please try again. Remember to evaluate \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(0,0) \) we have to substitute \(x=0\) and differentiate the resulting function of \(y\) with respect to \(y\).
